title: AP Environmental Science
summary: Trace ecosystem energy, population change, resource use and environmental impacts.
frameworkNote: Unit map checked against College Board on 15 October 2026 for the 2026-27 course. Each unit has one focused original revision lesson, not exhaustive topic coverage or an official practice paper. Uses the current nine-unit map and Fall 2026 CED listing. Numerical scenarios are original models; fieldwork and laboratory requirements remain separate.

modules.title: Productivity and trophic transfers
modules.focus: Account for respiration before estimating available biomass.
explanation: Gross primary productivity is the rate at which producers capture energy. Net primary productivity subtracts the producers’ own respiration and represents energy stored as new biomass. Report both the area and time basis when giving productivity units.

Consumers obtain only part of the energy at the previous trophic level. Unconsumed material, waste and respiration reduce transfer. Nutrients can cycle through decomposers, but usable energy continually enters and dissipates from the ecosystem.

workedExample.prompt: A grassland has gross productivity 1,200 and producer respiration 450 kJ/(m² year). Find net productivity.
steps: Subtract producer respiration: 1,200-450=750 kJ/(m² year).
This is the modelled energy stored in new producer biomass, before consumer-transfer losses.

misconception.claim: Net primary productivity equals all incoming sunlight.
misconception.correction: It is captured chemical energy remaining after producer respiration.

questions.prompt: Producers store 6,000 kJ. If 15% transfers to herbivores, how much is transferred?
questions.hint: Use the stated efficiency rather than assuming 10%.

questions.prompt: Why is phosphorus often described without a major atmospheric gaseous phase in its cycle?
questions.hint: Compare rock and soil reservoirs with gas exchange.
questions.answer: Its major exchanges involve weathering, uptake, decomposition and sedimentation rather than a large gaseous atmospheric reservoir.
checkpoints: Describe return through decomposition or sedimentation.

questions.hint: Add respiration back to net production.
questions.prompt: NPP is 900 energy units and producer respiration is 400. Find GPP and the fraction of GPP retained as NPP.
hints: Add respiration back to net production.
Use gross production as the percentage denominator.

questions.hint: Compare adjacent production values.
questions.prompt: Herbivores produce 240 kJ and carnivores 36 kJ over the same area and year. Calculate transfer efficiency and explain why organism counts alone cannot replace these data.
questions.answer: Efficiency is 36/240×100=15%. Counts ignore differences in body size, energy content and production over time.
checkpoints: Preserve matching area and time boundaries.
Explain why counts do not measure production energy.
hints: Compare adjacent production values.
Consider a few large organisms versus many small ones.

notes.title: Reasoning through productivity and trophic transfers
paragraphs: Energy enters most ecosystems through photosynthesis and leaves usable biological stores through respiration and other transfers. Gross primary productivity measures total producer fixation; net primary productivity subtracts producer respiration and represents energy available for producer growth and consumers. Trophic-transfer efficiency compares production at adjacent levels, not the number of organisms or their individual sizes. The familiar ten-percent figure is an approximation rather than a universal constant. Nutrients can cycle through organisms and physical reservoirs, whereas energy flows through the system and becomes increasingly dispersed as heat. Keep area and time units consistent when comparing productivity measurements.

workedExamples.prompt: Producers fix 2000 kJ/(m² year) and respire 800. Herbivore production is 180 kJ/(m² year). Find NPP and transfer efficiency.
steps: Efficiency=180/1200×100=15%; use net producer production as the adjacent-level denominator.
workedExamples.conclusion: NPP is 1200 kJ/(m² year) and producer-to-herbivore production efficiency is 15%.

flashcards.back: Gross primary productivity minus producer respiration.

flashcards.front: Why is ten-percent transfer not a law?
flashcards.back: Actual efficiency varies among organisms and ecosystems.

flashcards.front: Does energy cycle like carbon atoms?
flashcards.back: No; energy flows and is dispersed as heat.

flashcards.front: Which quantities should be compared for trophic production efficiency?
flashcards.back: Production at adjacent trophic levels in matching units.

modules.title: Biodiversity and habitat fragmentation
modules.focus: Separate species richness from abundance patterns.
explanation: Species richness counts species, while evenness describes how individuals are distributed among them. Two habitats can have identical richness but different community structure. Genetic and ecosystem diversity add further dimensions beyond a simple species count.

Fragmentation reduces continuous habitat and can isolate populations. Corridors may support dispersal and gene flow, although their effects depend on species and landscape context. Island biogeography relates immigration and extinction to isolation and habitat size.

workedExample.prompt: Compare communities with species counts [25,25,25,25] and [97,1,1,1].
steps: Each contains four species, so richness is equal.
The first is more even because individuals are distributed equally instead of dominated by one species.

misconception.claim: Equal species richness means equal biodiversity in every sense.
misconception.correction: Evenness, genetic variation and habitat diversity can still differ.

questions.prompt: All else equal, which island is likely to receive more mainland immigrants: near or far?
questions.hint: Consider dispersal distance.
questions.answer: The nearer island.
checkpoints: Shorter distance tends to raise immigration.
State that this is a model holding other factors fixed.

questions.prompt: How could a habitat corridor help isolated populations?
questions.hint: Think about movement between patches.
questions.answer: It can allow dispersal and gene flow, reducing isolation.
checkpoints: Avoid claiming every species benefits equally.

questions.hint: Separate the numerical change from the conservation conclusion.
questions.prompt: A restoration raises recorded richness from 12 to 15 species. Calculate the percentage increase and name one reason the result does not by itself establish full biodiversity recovery.
questions.answer: The increase is 3/12×100=25%. Richness alone omits evenness, genetic variation or persistence, and survey effort must be comparable.
checkpoints: Give a specific limitation of richness-only evidence.
hints: Separate the numerical change from the conservation conclusion.
Consider what a count leaves unmeasured.

questions.hint: Keep claims matched to the measured variable.
questions.prompt: A corridor increases animal crossings but not breeding success during one season. What conclusion is supported, and what remains uncertain?
questions.answer: The observations support improved movement during the measured season. They do not yet establish increased reproduction or long-term population recovery.
hints: Keep claims matched to the measured variable.
One season is not a long-term population trajectory.

notes.title: Reasoning through biodiversity and habitat fragmentation
paragraphs: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and ecosystem variation, so a single species count captures only one part. Species richness counts taxa, while evenness describes the distribution of individuals among them. Habitat fragmentation can reduce patch size, increase edge exposure and limit movement among populations. A corridor may improve movement and gene flow, but its effectiveness depends on the species, habitat quality and barriers; it can also transmit disturbances or invasive species. Conservation comparisons need defined endpoints such as breeding success or occupancy, replicated monitoring and a meaningful time frame rather than assuming that any connected map guarantees recovery.

workedExamples.prompt: Two habitat surveys each find four species. Counts are [10,10,10,10] and [28,4,4,4]. Compare richness and dominance.
steps: Both have richness four. In the first, the largest species has 10/40=25% of individuals.
In the second, the largest has 28/40=70%, so it is more dominated and less even.
workedExamples.conclusion: Richness matches, but the second community has much lower evenness.

flashcards.back: The number of species recorded.
How evenly individuals are distributed across species.

flashcards.front: How can fragmentation affect gene flow?
flashcards.back: It can isolate populations and restrict movement.

flashcards.front: What evidence should evaluate a corridor?
flashcards.back: Species-specific movement and population outcomes over time.

modules.title: Population change and doubling time
modules.focus: Calculate a net rate before projecting growth.
explanation: Population size changes through births, deaths, immigration and emigration. A rate per thousand must be divided by ten to express the same annual change as a percentage, assuming the listed components use the same population and time basis.

Exponential growth assumes a constant proportional rate. The rule of 70 approximates doubling time in years as 70 divided by annual percentage growth for modest rates. Resource limits, changing fertility and migration can make long-range projections unsuitable.

workedExample.prompt: A population has annual birth and death rates of 24 and 14 per thousand, with no migration. Estimate doubling time if the rate persists.
steps: Net growth is 10 per thousand, or 1% per year.
The rule of 70 gives about 70 years, conditional on sustained exponential growth.

misconception.claim: A doubling-time estimate guarantees when the population will double.
misconception.correction: It is conditional on a stable growth-rate model.

questions.prompt: Births are 30 and deaths 10 per thousand annually, without migration. Find the percentage growth rate.
questions.hint: Subtract then convert per thousand to percent.
questions.answer: 2% per year.

questions.prompt: What does a broad base in an age-structure diagram suggest?
questions.hint: The base represents young cohorts.
questions.answer: A large young cohort that may contribute to future growth as it reaches reproductive age.
checkpoints: Do not infer an exact future rate from shape alone.

questions.hint: The rule uses percent, not per-thousand units.
questions.prompt: A population has birth and death rates 18 and 8 per thousand per year, with no migration. Estimate doubling time using the rule of 70.
questions.answer: Net growth is 10 per thousand=1% per year; estimated doubling time is 70/1=70 years if the rate persists.
checkpoints: Subtract rates to obtain 10 per thousand.
Apply the approximation with its constant-rate assumption.
hints: The rule uses percent, not per-thousand units.
Divide 70 by the annual percentage rate.

questions.hint: Use each population’s own starting size.
questions.prompt: A population grows by 50 individuals when it has 500, and another grows by 50 when it has 5000. Compare percentage growth.
questions.answer: The first grows 10%; the second grows 1%. Equal absolute increases do not imply equal per-capita growth.
hints: Use each population’s own starting size.
Compare rates after normalising.

notes.title: Reasoning through population change and doubling time
paragraphs: Population accounting combines births, deaths, immigration and emigration. A crude birth or death rate per thousand must be converted before treating it as a percentage. Exponential growth assumes a constant per-capita rate and no effective resource limitation; real populations often depart from it as conditions change. Logistic growth adds a carrying-capacity constraint, but carrying capacity itself can shift with resources and environmental conditions. Age structure can suggest future momentum because cohorts enter reproductive ages, yet it is not a guarantee of growth without information about survival, fertility and migration. Distinguish absolute annual change from percentage growth.

workedExamples.prompt: A town starts with 20,000 people, records 300 births, 180 deaths, 250 immigrants and 170 emigrants in one year. Find net change and growth rate.
steps: Net change=300−180+250−170=200 people.
Divide by the starting population: 200/20,000×100=1%.
workedExamples.conclusion: The population rises by 200 to 20,200, a 1% increase.

flashcards.front: What four flows change population size?
flashcards.back: Births, deaths, immigration and emigration.

flashcards.front: How is 15 per thousand expressed as a percentage?

flashcards.back: A constant per-capita growth rate over the interval.
No; it depends on environmental resources and conditions.

modules.title: Soil, infiltration and runoff
modules.focus: Explain a watershed response using physical properties.
explanation: Soil texture describes sand, silt and clay proportions, while structure describes how particles aggregate. Pore spaces affect infiltration, water retention and aeration. Compaction can reduce connected pore space and increase surface runoff during rainfall.

Watersheds route water toward common outlets. Vegetation can slow surface flow, stabilise soil and intercept rainfall. Impervious surfaces alter that balance, so comparisons should hold rainfall and watershed area consistent before attributing a change to land cover.

workedExample.prompt: Two equal plots receive 20 mm of rain. Runoff is 5 mm from vegetation and 14 mm from pavement. Compare runoff fractions.
steps: Vegetated runoff fraction is 5/20=25%; paved runoff fraction is 14/20=70%.
The paved plot routes a larger fraction into surface flow under the stated conditions.

misconception.claim: More rainfall must always mean more groundwater recharge.
misconception.correction: Recharge also depends on infiltration, soil, vegetation and surface cover.

questions.prompt: A 100 m² plot receives 0.02 m rainfall. Find rain volume.
questions.hint: Multiply area by depth.
questions.answer: 2 m³.

questions.prompt: Why can removing hillside vegetation increase sediment in a stream?
questions.hint: Connect roots and flow speed.
questions.answer: Less root binding and interception can increase erosion and transport soil into runoff.
checkpoints: Name a stabilising role of vegetation.

questions.hint: Keep area and depth units compatible.
questions.prompt: A 200 m² paved area receives 25 mm rain and produces 4 m³ runoff. Find the runoff fraction.
questions.answer: Rain input is 200×0.025=5 m³; runoff fraction is 4/5=0.80, or 80%.
hints: Keep area and depth units compatible.
Compare runoff volume with total input.

questions.hint: Trace material from slope to channel.
questions.prompt: Two equally wet hillsides receive the same rain. One loses ground cover. Explain a mechanism linking this change to higher downstream sediment load.
questions.answer: Loss of cover exposes soil to raindrop impact and removes root stabilisation; runoff can detach and transport more material into the stream.
checkpoints: Identify increased soil exposure or reduced root stabilisation.
Explain detachment and transport by water.
Connect transported mass to downstream load.
hints: Trace material from slope to channel.
Do not claim rainfall itself must increase.

notes.title: Reasoning through soil, infiltration and runoff
paragraphs: Water arriving at a land surface can infiltrate, run off, evaporate or remain temporarily stored. Soil texture affects pore sizes and movement, while structure, compaction, organic matter and existing moisture also influence infiltration. Vegetation can intercept rainfall and stabilise soil with roots; removing it can increase erosion even when rainfall totals stay unchanged. A simple event water balance must state which terms are ignored rather than interpreting all non-runoff water as permanent groundwater recharge. Sediment transport depends on flow energy and exposed material, so concentration and total sediment load answer different questions about a stream.

workedExamples.prompt: A 500 m² site receives 30 mm rain. During the event, 6 m³ runs off and evaporation is negligible. Find rain volume and remaining infiltration-plus-storage.
steps: Rain depth is 0.030 m, so volume is 500×0.030=15 m³.
Remaining water is 15−6=9 m³, or 60% of input; the data do not separate infiltration from temporary storage.
workedExamples.conclusion: Input is 15 m³ and 9 m³ remains in the combined infiltration/storage terms.

flashcards.front: What converts rainfall depth to volume?
flashcards.back: Multiply by the area after matching units.
It reduces connected pore space.
They stabilise soil and vegetation slows surface flow.

flashcards.front: Does non-runoff automatically equal groundwater recharge?
flashcards.back: No; storage, evaporation and shallow soil water may also matter.

modules.title: Irrigation and resource trade-offs
modules.focus: Compare useful delivery with total withdrawal.
explanation: An irrigation efficiency compares water reaching its intended use with the water withdrawn. A more efficient system can reduce withdrawals for a fixed crop demand, but total use also depends on cultivated area, crop choice and management.

Agricultural decisions have linked effects on water, soil and biodiversity. Excess irrigation in poorly drained settings can promote waterlogging or salinisation. Integrated pest management combines monitoring and multiple controls rather than relying only on repeated broad pesticide applications.

workedExample.prompt: A crop needs 600 L delivered. Compare withdrawal at 50% and 80% delivery efficiency.
steps: At 50%, required withdrawal is 600/0.50=1,200 L.
At 80%, it is 600/0.80=750 L, saving 450 L for the same delivered amount.

misconception.claim: Higher efficiency necessarily lowers total regional water use.
misconception.correction: Expansion or changed crops can offset savings per unit of production.

questions.prompt: A system withdraws 1,000 L and delivers 700 L to its intended use. Find efficiency.
questions.hint: Divide useful delivery by withdrawal.
checkpoints: Express the fraction as a percentage.

questions.prompt: Why can repeated irrigation cause soil salinity to rise?
questions.hint: Water and dissolved salts have different fates.
questions.answer: Evaporation and plant water uptake leave salts behind, especially when drainage and leaching are inadequate.
checkpoints: Explain accumulation rather than creation of salt.

questions.hint: Delivered divided by withdrawn gives efficiency.
questions.prompt: A system withdraws 2500 L and delivers 1750 L. Find efficiency and the withdrawal needed to deliver 1750 L at 87.5% efficiency.
questions.answer: Initial efficiency is 70%; new withdrawal is 1750/0.875=2000 L.
hints: Delivered divided by withdrawn gives efficiency.
Invert the relation for required withdrawal.

questions.hint: Track both factors of the total.
questions.prompt: A drip-irrigation upgrade lowers water use per hectare, but irrigated area doubles. Can total withdrawal be assumed to fall?
questions.answer: No. Total withdrawal is use per hectare multiplied by area; if use per hectare falls by less than half, doubling area raises total withdrawal.
checkpoints: State the per-area times area relationship.
Give the half-use threshold or an equivalent numerical example.
hints: Track both factors of the total.
A rate improvement can be outweighed by expansion.

notes.title: Reasoning through irrigation and resource trade-offs
paragraphs: Irrigation efficiency compares water delivered for an intended use with water withdrawn, but a farm-level saving does not automatically become a basin-level saving. Some apparent losses return to streams or aquifers and can be reused; reduced withdrawal may also encourage expansion of irrigated area. Evaluate consumption, return flows and the chosen system boundary. Salinisation develops when dissolved salts accumulate as water evaporates or is taken up, especially with inadequate drainage. Sustainable irrigation therefore involves both water quantity and soil conditions. A percentage efficiency gain should be checked against the actual withdrawal volume before comparing management options.

workedExamples.prompt: A field requires 1200 m³ delivered water. Compare withdrawals at 60% and 80% efficiency and calculate the reduction.
steps: Withdrawals are 1200/0.60=2000 m³ and 1200/0.80=1500 m³.
The reduction is 500 m³, or 500/2000×100=25%.
workedExamples.conclusion: Improved delivery efficiency reduces this field’s required withdrawal by 25% under fixed demand.

flashcards.back: Useful delivered amount divided by efficiency.

flashcards.front: Why might basin savings differ from farm savings?
flashcards.back: Return flows and changes in irrigated area can alter total consumption.

flashcards.front: What remains when irrigation water evaporates?
flashcards.back: Dissolved salts can remain in the soil.
Changing demand changes the withdrawal comparison.

modules.title: Energy efficiency and electricity demand
explanation: Power is the rate of energy transfer. Electrical energy in kilowatt-hours equals power in kilowatts times operating hours. Efficiency is useful output divided by input; conserving energy usually means reducing required input for a given service.

Comparing energy sources requires a defined boundary. Operational emissions, material extraction, land use and reliability address different parts of the system. A renewable source can still have environmental costs, so explain the particular trade-off rather than using a single label as a verdict.

workedExample.prompt: A 60 W lamp is replaced by a 10 W lamp providing the same light for 5 hours daily. Find daily electricity savings.
steps: The power reduction is 50 W=0.050 kW.
Daily savings are 0.050(5)=0.25 kWh.

misconception.claim: A kilowatt and a kilowatt-hour measure the same quantity.
misconception.correction: A kilowatt is power; a kilowatt-hour is energy.

questions.prompt: A 2 kW heater operates for 3 hours. Find electricity use.
questions.hint: Multiply power by time.
questions.answer: 6 kWh.

questions.prompt: An engine takes 1,000 J and supplies 300 J useful work. Find efficiency and remaining energy.
questions.hint: Apply energy conservation.
questions.answer: 30% efficient; 700 J goes to other transfers, mainly heat.

questions.hint: Use time in hours.
questions.prompt: A 500 W device runs for 4 hours. Find electricity use and useful output if efficiency is 80%.
questions.answer: Input is 0.500×4=2 kWh; useful output is 1.6 kWh and the remainder is 0.4 kWh.
checkpoints: Apply efficiency to obtain 1.6 kWh useful output.
hints: Use time in hours.
Efficiency multiplies energy input.

questions.hint: Multiply intensity by activity level.
questions.prompt: A device uses 25% less energy per unit of service, reducing input per unit from 4 to 3 kWh. Service use rises from 10 to 16 units. Compare total input.
questions.answer: Input rises from 40 to 48 kWh, a 20% increase; lower energy per unit is outweighed by greater use.
checkpoints: Calculate the 20% increase and explain the two-factor change.
hints: Multiply intensity by activity level.
Use the original total as the percentage denominator.

notes.title: Reasoning through energy efficiency and electricity demand
paragraphs: Power is a rate of energy transfer, while electricity consumption is energy accumulated over time. Multiply kilowatts by hours to obtain kilowatt-hours, and convert watts to kilowatts first. Efficiency compares useful output with input using matching energy units. An efficient device can still consume substantial energy if used for longer or at a larger scale. Comparing technologies also needs consistent service, such as equal lighting or heating delivered, and an explicit boundary for production, operation and disposal. Electricity-related emissions depend on the generation mix and timing, so energy savings alone do not establish one universal emissions reduction.

workedExamples.prompt: A 1.5 kW appliance runs for 2 hours daily. A replacement provides the same service using 1.0 kW for that period. Find energy saved over 30 days.
steps: Daily saving=(1.5−1.0)×2=1.0 kWh.
Over 30 days, saving is 30 kWh; if an explicitly assumed factor is 0.4 kg CO₂/kWh, associated operational reduction is 12 kg CO₂.
workedExamples.conclusion: The replacement saves 30 kWh, corresponding to 12 kg CO₂ only under the stated factor.

flashcards.back: Power, a rate of energy transfer.
Energy.
Useful output divided by input.
Otherwise a lower input may simply reflect less useful output.

modules.title: Primary emissions and secondary air pollution
modules.focus: Trace the chemical pathway from source to pollutant.
explanation: A primary pollutant is emitted directly, while a secondary pollutant forms through environmental reactions. Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant associated with reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds in sunlight.

Air pollution concentration depends on emissions and dispersion. A temperature inversion can restrict vertical mixing and trap pollutants near the surface. A control should target its mechanism: reducing a precursor, capturing particles or changing a combustion process addresses different sources.

workedExample.prompt: A city sees high ozone on sunny afternoons despite low direct ozone emissions. Explain why.
steps: Ozone can form secondarily from emitted precursors reacting in sunlight.
Low direct ozone emissions therefore do not rule out substantial ground-level ozone concentrations.

misconception.claim: All ozone has the same environmental role regardless of altitude.
misconception.correction: Stratospheric ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation; ground-level ozone is an air pollutant.

questions.prompt: Why can an inversion worsen a pollution episode?
questions.hint: Consider vertical air mixing.
questions.answer: It suppresses vertical mixing, allowing pollutants to accumulate near the ground.
checkpoints: Keep emission rate distinct from concentration.

questions.prompt: A filter lowers particle emissions from 80 to 20 kg/day. Find percentage reduction.
questions.hint: Use the initial amount as denominator.
Separate an absolute difference from a fraction.
questions.prompt: A control lowers emissions from 120 to 90 kg/day. Find absolute and percentage reduction.
questions.answer: The reduction is 30 kg/day, or 30/120×100=25%.
hints: Separate an absolute difference from a fraction.
Do not divide by the final emissions.

questions.hint: Consider a factor that changed alongside the intervention.
questions.prompt: An air-quality monitor improves after a control is introduced, but the same week becomes much windier. Why is a causal claim uncertain?
questions.answer: Wind can increase dispersion independently of the control. Comparable meteorological conditions, additional sites or a suitable comparison period are needed to separate the effects.
checkpoints: Identify wind as an alternative explanation.
Propose a comparison that addresses weather.
hints: Consider a factor that changed alongside the intervention.
The monitor records the combined effects of emissions and transport.

notes.title: Reasoning through primary emissions and secondary air pollution
paragraphs: Primary air pollutants are emitted directly, while secondary pollutants form through atmospheric reactions. Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant produced through photochemical reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds; its abundance cannot be inferred from direct ozone emissions alone. Weather affects transport and dilution, so a temperature inversion can trap pollution near the surface without creating the emissions itself. Exposure also depends on where people spend time and on concentration duration. Evaluating a control requires an emissions measure, an ambient concentration measure and attention to meteorology, because a favourable weather period can mimic an apparent treatment effect.

workedExamples.prompt: A factory emits particles at 50 kg/day before control and 15 kg/day after. Nearby concentration falls from 40 to 32 μg/m³. Compare percentage changes.
steps: Emissions fall by (50−15)/50×100=70%.
Ambient concentration falls by (40−32)/40×100=20%; other sources and atmospheric conditions affect the concentration response.
workedExamples.conclusion: Emissions decrease 70%, while the observed ambient concentration decreases 20%.

flashcards.back: A substance emitted directly.
It forms through atmospheric chemical reactions.

flashcards.front: How can an inversion worsen near-surface pollution?
flashcards.back: It suppresses vertical mixing.

flashcards.front: Why separate emissions from ambient concentration?
flashcards.back: Transport, weather and other sources affect the latter.

modules.title: Nutrient pollution and oxygen demand
modules.focus: Connect excess nutrients to aquatic oxygen loss.
explanation: Nutrient enrichment can stimulate algal growth. When biomass dies, decomposers consume dissolved oxygen during respiration, potentially causing hypoxia. The chain involves biological oxygen demand; nutrients do not simply remove all oxygen by being present.

Pollution can come from a discrete outlet or diffuse runoff across a landscape. Management should address the source and transport pathway. Concentration alone is not pollutant load: load also depends on water flow, so dilution can lower concentration without reducing the mass released.

workedExample.prompt: A stream carries 2 mg/L nitrate at 1,000 L/min. Calculate nitrate load.
steps: Multiply concentration by flow: 2(1,000)=2,000 mg/min.
Convert units to obtain 2 g/min.

misconception.claim: A lower concentration always means less pollutant mass enters a river.
misconception.correction: A higher flow can offset the concentration decrease; compare loads.

questions.prompt: What process directly increases oxygen demand after an algal bloom dies?
questions.hint: Follow the organic matter into decomposers.
questions.answer: Microbial respiration during decomposition.
checkpoints: Connect respiration to dissolved oxygen consumption.

questions.prompt: A concentration is 3 mg/L at 500 L/min. Find load in g/min.
questions.hint: Multiply before converting milligrams.
questions.answer: 1.5 g/min.

questions.hint: Cancel litres when multiplying.
questions.prompt: Water carries 5 mg/L of a pollutant at 400 L/min. Find load in g/min and mass transported in one hour at constant conditions.
questions.answer: Load is 2000 mg/min=2 g/min; one-hour mass is 120 g.
hints: Cancel litres when multiplying.
Convert time only after calculating the rate.

questions.hint: Trace oxygen use after organisms die.
questions.prompt: A lake has abundant algae and declining dissolved oxygen after a large die-off. Give a causal explanation and one measurement that would strengthen it.
questions.answer: Decomposers consume oxygen while processing dead organic matter. Measurements of decomposition-related oxygen demand alongside oxygen over time would test this pathway, while temperature and mixing should also be considered.
checkpoints: Identify microbial decomposition of dead biomass.
Connect aerobic respiration to oxygen consumption.
Propose a relevant measurement or controlled comparison.
hints: Trace oxygen use after organisms die.
A causal explanation should suggest observable evidence.

notes.title: Reasoning through nutrient pollution and oxygen demand
paragraphs: Pollutant concentration describes mass per volume, while load describes mass passing a location per time. Multiplying concentration by water flow gives load, so a diluted stream can still transport more pollutant if its flow rises enough. Nutrient enrichment can stimulate algal production; later decomposition consumes dissolved oxygen and can harm organisms that require it. Temperature and mixing also affect oxygen conditions, so a bloom alone does not specify every downstream outcome. Management should trace nutrient sources, transport and biological responses. Sampling at only one flow condition may miss storm-driven loads that dominate the annual total.

workedExamples.prompt: A stream’s concentration falls from 4 to 2 mg/L while flow rises from 200 to 600 L/min. Compare pollutant loads.
steps: Initial load is 4×200=800 mg/min=0.8 g/min.
Final load is 2×600=1200 mg/min=1.2 g/min, a 50% increase despite lower concentration.
workedExamples.conclusion: The concentration halves but the transported load rises by 50%.

flashcards.back: Mass transported per unit time.
Concentration multiplied by flow rate.

flashcards.front: What consumes oxygen after dead algae accumulate?
flashcards.back: Aerobic microbial decomposition.
High flows can transport large nutrient or sediment loads.

modules.title: Carbon feedbacks and ocean chemistry
modules.focus: Distinguish a forcing from a feedback response.
explanation: Greenhouse gases absorb and emit infrared radiation, altering Earth’s energy balance. A feedback occurs when the resulting change influences the original process. For example, melting reflective ice can reduce reflectivity and increase absorbed sunlight.

Dissolved carbon dioxide changes seawater carbonate chemistry, raising hydrogen-ion concentration and reducing carbonate availability under typical conditions. Ocean acidification means a decline in pH; seawater need not cross below pH 7 for this term to apply.

workedExample.prompt: Explain why ice-albedo change can amplify an initial warming.
steps: Warming melts some reflective ice and exposes darker surfaces.
Those surfaces absorb more sunlight, creating an additional warming influence: a positive feedback.

misconception.claim: Ocean acidification means every ocean sample has pH below 7.
misconception.correction: It refers to decreasing pH relative to the prior state, even while water remains alkaline.

questions.prompt: Why is increased plant uptake of CO₂ potentially a negative climate feedback?
questions.hint: Trace how the response affects the initial forcing.
questions.answer: If warming or CO₂ increases uptake, that uptake can reduce atmospheric CO₂ growth and oppose some warming.

questions.prompt: Atmospheric carbon input is 12 units/year and removal is 7 units/year. Find net accumulation.
questions.hint: Subtract removal from input.
questions.answer: 5 units/year.
checkpoints: Positive net flow increases the reservoir.

questions.hint: Integrate the constant rate over five years.
questions.prompt: A carbon stock begins at 100 units and has constant net inflow 3 units/year for five years. Find the final stock and distinguish stock from flow.
questions.answer: The final stock is 115 units. Stock is the stored amount; 3 units/year is the rate at which it changes.
checkpoints: Distinguish amount from rate with units.
hints: Integrate the constant rate over five years.
The initial stock is not itself a yearly flow.

questions.hint: Feedback sign describes direction, not guaranteed dominance.
questions.prompt: A warming response causes extra plant carbon uptake. Under what condition is this a negative feedback, and why does that not prove total warming stops?
questions.answer: It is negative feedback if the uptake reduces atmospheric CO₂ relative to what it otherwise would be, opposing the initial warming. Its magnitude and persistence may be insufficient to offset other forcing and feedbacks.
checkpoints: Connect uptake to reduced atmospheric CO₂ relative to a baseline.
Explain opposition to the initial warming.
State the magnitude or persistence limitation.
hints: Feedback sign describes direction, not guaranteed dominance.
Compare the response with the full system balance.

notes.title: Reasoning through carbon feedbacks and ocean chemistry
paragraphs: Climate feedbacks respond to an initial change and either amplify or oppose it; they are distinct from the initial forcing. Warming can reduce reflective snow and ice, increasing absorbed sunlight and reinforcing warming. Carbon-cycle responses can act in different directions and have limits, so increased plant uptake should not be assumed to offset all emissions. When atmospheric CO₂ dissolves in seawater it shifts carbonate chemistry towards greater hydrogen-ion concentration and lower carbonate-ion availability. The ocean can remain above neutral pH while becoming more acidic, because acidification refers to a pH decrease rather than a requirement to cross pH seven.

workedExamples.prompt: A carbon reservoir receives 18 units/year and releases 11. An intervention reduces input by 4 units/year with release unchanged. Find accumulation before and after.
steps: Initial net accumulation is 18−11=7 units/year.
New input is 14, giving 14−11=3 units/year; the stock still grows, but more slowly.
workedExamples.conclusion: Accumulation falls from 7 to 3 units/year without becoming a net decline.

flashcards.back: A response that amplifies an initial change.

flashcards.front: Why can melting ice reinforce warming?
flashcards.back: Lower reflectivity increases absorbed solar energy.

flashcards.front: Does slower accumulation mean a falling stock?
flashcards.back: No; the net flow must become negative.

flashcards.front: Can seawater acidify while pH stays above seven?
flashcards.back: Yes; acidification means pH decreases.
